'''Washington Irving Stringham''' (December 10, 1847 – October 5, 1909) was an American mathematician born in [[Yorkshire, New York|Yorkshire]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. He was the first person to denote the [[natural logarithm]] as <math>\ln(x)</math> where <math>x</math> is its argument. The use of <math>\ln(x)</math> in place of <math>\log_e(x)</math> is commonplace in [[calculator|digital calculators]] today.

<blockquote>
"In place of <math>^{e}\log</math> we shall henceforth use the shorter symbol <math>\ln</math>, made up of the initial letters of ''logarithm'' and of ''natural'' or ''Napierian''."<ref>Charles Smith, Irving Stringham, ''Elementary algebra for the use of schools and colleges'' 2nd ed, (The Macmillan Company, New York, 1904) p 437.</ref>
</blockquote>

Stringham graduated from [[Harvard College]] in 1877. He earned his PhD from [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1880. His dissertation was titled ''Regular Figures in N-dimensional Space''<ref>W.I. Stringham "Regular Figures in N-dimensional Space", ''American Journal of Mathematics'' Vol 3 (1880) pp 1-15.</ref> under his advisor [[James Joseph Sylvester]].

In 1881 he was in Schwartzbach, [[Saxony]], when he submitted an article on [[finite group]]s found in the [[quaternion]] algebra.<ref>I. Stringham (1881) "Determination of the finite quaternion groups", [[American Journal of Mathematics]] 4(1–4):345–57 {{doi|10.2307/2369172}}</ref>

Stringham began his professorship in mathematics at [[University of California at Berkeley|Berkeley]] in 1882.<ref>"In Memoriam, Dean Stringham" ''University of California Chronicle'' Vol XII (University Press, Berkeley, 1909) pp 1–20.</ref> In 1893 in Chicago, his paper ''Formulary for an Introduction to Elliptic Functions'' was read at the International Mathematical Congress held in connection with the [[World's Columbian Exposition]].<ref>{{cite book|chapter=''Formulary for an Introduction to Elliptic Functions'' by Irving Stringham|title=Mathematical papers read at the International Mathematical Congress held in connection with the World's Columbian Exposition|year=1896|pages=350–366|location=NY|publisher=Macmillan as publisher for the AMS|url=http://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.b3841648;view=1up;seq=372}}</ref> In 1900 he was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in Paris.<ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cF1tAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA327|pages=327–338|year=1902|volume=Tome 2|title=Compte rendu du deuxième Congrès international des mathématiciens tenu à Paris du 6 au 12 Aout 1900|chapter=''Orthogonal transformations in elliptic, or in hyperbolic, space'' by Irving Stringham}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Irving married Martha Sherman Day. The couple raised a daughter, Martha Sherman Stringham, (March 5, 1891- August 7, 1967).
